title: Cache Performance Analysis: AMAT and the Memory Hierarchy

sections.heading: Hit time, miss rate, miss penalty
sections.body:
Cache performance boils down to three numbers and one equation that combines them.

**Miss rate** $m$ is the fraction of references that miss: misses divided by total references, so the hit rate is $1-m$. CENG331's slides quote 3–10% as typical for an L1 cache and well under 1% for an L2, though the exact figure depends entirely on the program.

**Hit time** $T_h$ is the time to deliver a word that *is* in the cache to the CPU. It already includes the work of determining whether the access is a hit — set selection and tag comparison — not just the data transfer. The i7's L1 answers in 4 cycles; the idealized teaching examples below use 1–2.

**Miss penalty** $T_p$ is the *additional* time charged only when a reference misses. Typical values run 50–200 cycles to main memory, and the trend is upward, since DRAM latency has not kept pace with clock rates.

These combine into the average memory access time:

$$\text{AMAT} = T_h + m \cdot T_p$$

Every reference pays $T_h$; only the $m$ fraction that miss also pay $T_p$. Writing the same quantity as $(1-m)T_h + m(T_h+T_p)$ makes this obvious — multiplying out returns exactly the compact form, so a hit never owes $T_p$, and a miss still owes $T_h$, because the cache has to be checked before a miss can even be declared.

The formula also explains why the course insists on quoting miss rate rather than hit rate. With $T_h=1$ and $T_p=100$: at 97% hits, $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.03\times100 = 4$ cycles; at 99% hits, $\text{AMAT} = 1 + 0.01\times100 = 2$ cycles. A rise from 97% to 99% looks like a two-point improvement, but it halves AMAT, because $\partial\text{AMAT}/\partial m = T_p$ is large: every remaining point of miss rate is disproportionately expensive.

sections.heading: Multi-level caches: local versus global miss rate
sections.body:
A modern machine chains several caches, and the penalty term of one level is not a constant — it is the average access time of the level below it:

$$\text{AMAT}_k = T_{h,k} + m_k \cdot \text{AMAT}_{k+1}$$

with the recursion terminating at $\text{AMAT}_{\text{last}+1} = T_{\text{DRAM}}$, the cost of a reference that misses every cache in the hierarchy.

The rate $m_k$ here is the **local** miss rate: misses at level $k$ divided only by the references that actually reached level $k$, i.e. that already missed at level $k-1$. That is different from the **global** miss rate $g_k = m_1 m_2 \cdots m_k$, which divides by every reference the CPU issues. Expanding the recursion gives an equivalent flat sum

$$\text{AMAT} = T_{h,1} + \sum_{k \ge 1} g_k \, T_{h,k+1}$$

reading $T_{h,\text{last}+1}$ as the DRAM latency. Confusing the two rates is the most common error on this material: an L2 with a local miss rate of 25–40% is completely normal, since L1 has already filtered out every reference with easy locality and only the hard residue reaches L2. What matters for the program's actual memory traffic is $g_2 = m_1 m_2$, typically well under 1%.

The course's running example is the Intel Core i7: a private, per-core 32 KB, 8-way L1 i-cache and d-cache at 4 cycles; a private, per-core 256 KB, 8-way unified L2 at 11 cycles; and an 8 MB, 16-way L3 shared across all cores at 30–40 cycles — all on-chip, with a uniform 64-byte block at every level. CS:APP's Figure 6.39 for the same chip lists slightly different numbers (L2 at 10 cycles, L3 at 40–75), a discrepancy worth stating explicitly on an exam rather than silently picking one.

sections.heading: The three Cs: diagnosing where a miss comes from
sections.body:
To fix a miss rate you first have to know which of three causes produced it.

A **cold** (compulsory) miss is the first reference to a block: the cache started empty, and no organization could have prevented it. Scanning an array of $w$-byte elements with $B$-byte blocks touches a fresh block once every $B/w$ elements, so the compulsory miss rate is $w/B$ — a property of block size alone.

A **capacity** miss occurs because the working set of blocks in active use exceeds the cache's size; it would still occur in a fully associative cache of the same capacity, so it answers to cache size, or, on the programmer's side, to shrinking the working set.

A **conflict** miss occurs when the cache is large enough overall but the mapping function crowds several live blocks into the same set. The course's canonical example: if block $i$ must live in set $i \bmod 4$, referencing blocks $0, 8, 0, 8, \ldots$ misses on every single access, even though at most one block is ever live. Conflict misses answer to associativity.

The classification is relative to a baseline, and it is worth internalizing exactly how: a miss counts as "conflict" precisely when it would have hit in a fully associative cache of equal capacity under an *optimal* replacement policy. Swap in ordinary LRU for that oracle and the comparison can flip entirely — a cyclic pattern whose period exceeds the number of ways by one makes LRU miss on every access, so a direct-mapped cache can legitimately beat a fully associative LRU cache of the same capacity on that stream. The three Cs are a diagnostic vocabulary tied to a baseline, not an absolute accounting.

sections.heading: Block size, associativity, cache size: what each buys and costs
sections.body:
Every design parameter trades one term of the AMAT equation for another.

**Cache size.** A bigger cache raises the hit rate by holding more of the working set, but large memories are physically harder to access quickly, so it also raises hit time. That single trade-off explains the whole hierarchy's shape: L1 stays small because it must answer in a handful of cycles, and L3 can afford to be large because it only has to beat main memory.

**Block size.** Larger blocks push the compulsory miss rate down (it scales as $w/B$) by exploiting spatial locality. But for a fixed cache size, larger blocks mean fewer lines, which can hurt programs whose locality is mostly temporal rather than spatial, and larger blocks take longer to transfer on a miss, raising the miss penalty. The i7 settles on 64 bytes at every level as that compromise.

**Associativity.** Raising $E$, the number of lines per set, reduces vulnerability to conflict misses, since more of them can hold blocks that would otherwise collide. It is not free: more tag bits, more replacement-state bits and more parallel comparators per set add hit-time complexity, and can slow victim selection on a miss. CS:APP frames the resolution as hit-time-versus-miss-penalty: keep associativity low near the top, where the miss penalty is only a handful of cycles and hit time dominates, and raise it further down, where a slower hit barely registers against a much larger penalty. On the i7, L1 and L2 are 8-way and L3 is 16-way.

**Write policy.** Write-through caches are simpler and pair with a write buffer that updates memory independently; write-back caches produce far fewer transfers, which matters more the further down the hierarchy you go. CS:APP recommends reasoning about your own code as though every level were write-back with write-allocate — the industry trend, and symmetric with reads.

sections.heading: Software locality: loop order, stride and blocking
sections.body:
The model becomes actionable the moment you can read a miss rate off a loop nest, and for C arrays — stored row-major, so `a[i][j]` sits at $\text{base} + (iN+j)\cdot\text{sizeof(elem)}$ — that reading is mechanical. Walking `j` for fixed `i` is a stride-1 scan: one miss every $B/\text{sizeof(elem)}$ elements, a miss rate of $\text{sizeof(elem)}/B$. Walking `i` for fixed `j` strides by $N\cdot\text{sizeof(elem)}$ bytes; once that exceeds the block size, every access lands in a fresh block and the miss rate is 1 — the same data, the same number of operations, radically different memory traffic.

The slides apply this to matrix multiplication under a fixed set of assumptions — 32-byte blocks (four 8-byte doubles), $N$ large enough that $1/N \approx 0$, and a cache too small to hold multiple rows — and simply read the inner loop of each ordering. For the standard `ijk` order, `a[i][k]` strides by one element (miss rate $8/32 = 0.25$ per access), `b[k][j]` strides by $N$ elements (miss rate 1 per access), and `c[i][j]`/`sum` stays in a register throughout (rate 0): 1.25 misses per inner-loop iteration. Reordering to `kij` holds `a[i][k]` fixed across the inner loop while both `b[k][j]` and `c[i][j]` become stride-1, cutting the total to 0.5 misses per iteration. The arithmetic performed is identical in every ordering — only the memory traffic changes.

Reordering fixes spatial locality only; reusing data before it is evicted needs **blocking**: partition the matrices into $t \times t$ tiles small enough that the three active tiles fit in cache together, so each tile is loaded once and reused $t$ times instead of once per pass. The **memory mountain** — measured read throughput plotted against working-set size and access stride — is the experimental counterpart: ridges along the size axis mark where the working set stops fitting in L1, then L2, then L3 (temporal locality), and slopes along the stride axis show throughput falling once the stride outruns the block size (spatial locality).

complexity.notes: Already includes hit/miss determination, not just transfer
Local L1 miss rate 3–10% is typical
Private per core, unified instructions + data
Local L2 miss rate of 25–40% is routine, not a defect
Reached only on $g_3=m_1m_2m_3$ of references, yet often dominates AMAT
Depends on block size only, not on $E$ or $S$

code.caption: A direct-mapped (S=4, B=2) cache simulator that decomposes each address into tag/set/offset by shifting and masking, then replays the CENG331 exam's column-wise scan of a 5×5 char matrix at address 0. Verified output: 10 hits, 15 misses, 60% miss rate.

worked_example.problem:
A machine models its Core i7-style hierarchy with the slide values $T_{h,1}=4$, $T_{h,2}=11$, $T_{h,3}=35$ cycles (the midpoint of the quoted 30–40 cycle L3 range) and a DRAM access of 200 cycles. For one workload the local miss rates are $m_1=5\%$, $m_2=30\%$, $m_3=50\%$.

1. Compute AMAT via the recursion, and check it against the flat global-rate form.
2. The workload issues 1.2 memory references per instruction and would run at CPI 1.0 if every reference hit in L1 (the L1 hit itself is fully pipelined). What is the real CPI?
3. Two proposals promise to lower this CPI: (A) halve the L1 miss rate to 2.5% by restructuring loops, leaving $\text{AMAT}_2$ unchanged; or (B) halve the DRAM latency to 100 cycles with faster memory, which changes $\text{AMAT}_2$ and $\text{AMAT}_3$. Which gives the larger speedup?
worked_example.solution:
**1. AMAT.** Unwind the recursion bottom-up:

$$\text{AMAT}_3 = 35 + 0.50 \times 200 = 135 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{AMAT}_2 = 11 + 0.30 \times 135 = 51.5 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{AMAT} = 4 + 0.05 \times 51.5 = 6.575 \text{ cycles}$$

The global rates are $g_1 = m_1 = 0.05$, $g_2 = m_1 m_2 = 0.015$, $g_3 = m_1 m_2 m_3 = 0.0075$, and the flat form agrees:

$$4 + 0.05(11) + 0.015(35) + 0.0075(200) = 6.575 \text{ cycles} \ \checkmark$$

**2. CPI.** Only the fraction of references that miss L1 stalls the pipeline, and each such stall costs $\text{AMAT}_2$ — everything below L1:

$$\text{stalls/instr} = 1.2 \times 0.05 \times 51.5 = 3.09$$

$$\text{CPI} = 1.0 + 3.09 = 4.09$$

**3. Which proposal wins?** Proposal A leaves $\text{AMAT}_2 = 51.5$ untouched and only lowers $m_1$:

$$\text{CPI}_A = 1.0 + 1.2 \times 0.025 \times 51.5 = 2.545$$

$$\text{speedup}_A = 4.09 / 2.545 \approx 1.61\times$$

Proposal B rebuilds the recursion with the faster DRAM:

$$\text{AMAT}_{3,B} = 35 + 0.50 \times 100 = 85 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{AMAT}_{2,B} = 11 + 0.30 \times 85 = 36.5 \text{ cycles}$$

$$\text{CPI}_B = 1.0 + 1.2 \times 0.05 \times 36.5 = 3.19$$

$$\text{speedup}_B = 4.09 / 3.19 \approx 1.28\times$$

**Proposal A wins by a wide margin.** The reason is structural, not a coincidence of these particular numbers: $m_1$ is the outermost multiplier in the recursion, so it scales the *entire* $\text{AMAT}_2$ term beneath it, while DRAM sits behind two levels of filtering and is reached on only $g_3 = 0.75\%$ of references — halving its latency removes at most $g_3 \times 100 = 0.75$ cycles from AMAT. A miss rate near the CPU is leveraged by everything beneath it; a latency far from the CPU is discounted by everything above it.

pitfalls: **Confusing local and global miss rate.** An L2 local miss rate of 30% is normal, not a design flaw — L1 already absorbed the easy references. The recursive AMAT form takes *local* rates; the flat sum takes *global* ones ($g_k = m_1\cdots m_k$). Mixing them inflates the answer by orders of magnitude.

**Dropping the hit time from the miss path.** $\text{AMAT}=T_h+mT_p$ already charges $T_h$ on every access, because a miss is only known to be a miss after the lookup fails. Writing $(1-m)T_h + mT_p$ silently skips the hit-time cost on the miss path.

**Treating the miss penalty as one constant in a multi-level hierarchy.** There is no single number: an L1 miss costs $\text{AMAT}_2$, which itself depends on $m_2$, $m_3$ and the DRAM latency. Quoting "the" miss penalty only makes sense for a single-level cache.

**Assuming a bigger block is always better.** It lowers the compulsory rate as $w/B$, but at fixed capacity it leaves fewer lines — worse for temporal locality — and it lengthens the transfer, raising the miss penalty. There is an optimum, and on current hardware it sits at 64 bytes.

**Reading AMAT as wall-clock time.** It is an average *latency*; an out-of-order core overlaps independent misses with each other and with other work. A loop with high memory-level parallelism can absorb misses AMAT charges in full, while a pointer-chasing loop, where each miss depends on the previous one's result, cannot. AMAT ranks designs — it does not predict execution time by itself.
applications: **Tuned linear-algebra libraries** (OpenBLAS, BLIS, Intel MKL) pick GEMM tile sizes directly from this model — one tile dimension chosen to fit L1, an outer tile to fit L2 — turning the same $O(N^3)$ arithmetic into an order-of-magnitude faster kernel purely by cutting $m$.

**Hardware performance counters** (`perf stat -e cache-references,cache-misses,LLC-load-misses`) measure local and global miss rates on a running binary, turning the AMAT formula from a homework exercise into an actual profiling technique for deciding whether a slow loop is memory-bound at all.

**Database storage engines** size their units of work to the hierarchy: column-store execution processes vectors small enough to stay resident in L2, and B-tree node sizes are chosen so a single node read touches only a handful of cache lines per level of the tree.

**The Linux kernel** declares hot per-CPU structures `__cacheline_aligned` so that two cores' data never share a 64-byte line; without it, coherence traffic between cores shows up in profiling as an inexplicably inflated miss rate — false sharing.
**Compiler loop optimizations** — loop interchange, tiling, prefetch insertion — applied by GCC and LLVM at `-O2`/`-O3` automate exactly the loop-reordering and blocking argument in this card.
exam_focus: The 2018 CENG331 final gave a 5×5 `char matrix` at address 0, summed **column-wise** (`col` outer, `row` inner), on a cold, direct-mapped cache with 4 sets and 2-byte blocks, and asked for a filled-in 5×5 grid of h/m — exactly the computation the code listing on this card performs (10 hits, 15 misses, verified by simulation).

The last CENG331 quiz combined a cache and a TLB on one IA32 system (1 KB direct-mapped cache, 16-byte blocks, 1 KB pages, an 8-entry direct-mapped TLB, a one-level page table) and asked for both TLB and L1 miss counts over a full row-major scan of a 1024×1024 array, then a separate miss count for a loop alternating between two fixed addresses — an answer that depends entirely on whether those two addresses land in the same cache set.

The slides drill one AMAT example until it is automatic: hit time 1 cycle, miss penalty 100 cycles, giving 4 cycles of AMAT at a 97% hit rate and 2 cycles at 99% — offered explicitly to justify why the course reports miss rate rather than hit rate.

The slides and CS:APP disagree slightly on the same Core i7 (L2: 11 vs. 10 cycles; L3: 30–40 vs. 40–75 cycles); state which source you are using rather than silently picking one — exam credit is for the recursion, not the exact constant.

self_check.question: A colleague measures a 30% miss rate at L2 and concludes the cache is poorly designed. What is wrong with that conclusion, and what should they report instead?
self_check.answer: Nothing is necessarily wrong. 30% is the **local** miss rate — misses at L2 divided by the references that reached L2, which are only the ones L1 already failed on. L1 filters out everything with easy locality, so a high local rate at L2 is expected; 25–40% is routine. The number that describes the *program's* behavior is the **global** miss rate $g_2 = m_1 m_2$: with a typical $m_1=5\%$, $g_2 = 0.05\times0.30 = 1.5\%$, i.e. fewer than 2 references in 100 get past L2 at all. And the number that describes *cost* is neither rate alone but its contribution to AMAT through $g_2\,T_{h,3}$ — judging a level in isolation from the rates above and below it is meaningless.

self_check.question: For the 5×5 `char matrix` summed column-wise on a direct-mapped cache with 4 sets and 2-byte blocks (matrix at address 0, cold cache), how many hits and misses occur, and how do the misses split across the three Cs?
self_check.answer:
`matrix[row][col]` sits at address $5\cdot\text{row}+\text{col}$; the access order is column by column, so addresses run $0,5,10,15,20,\,1,6,11,16,21,\ldots$ Working out set $=\lfloor \text{addr}/2\rfloor \bmod 4$ for all 25 accesses (or running the simulator in this card) gives **10 hits and 15 misses**, a 60% miss rate.

To split the misses: 13 distinct 2-byte blocks are touched (25 bytes across blocks of 2), so there are exactly **13 cold misses**. Simulating an *optimal* (Belady) fully associative cache of the same 8-byte capacity on the same block sequence gives 14 misses total, i.e. one miss beyond the 13 unavoidable cold ones — **1 capacity miss**. The direct-mapped cache takes one further miss beyond that optimal bound — **1 conflict miss** — caused by two blocks that are both live but happen to map to the same set.

A useful check on how baseline-dependent this classification is: the same fully associative cache under ordinary **LRU**, rather than an optimal oracle, misses on all 25 accesses — worse than the direct-mapped cache's 15. The block sequence cycles with a period just over 4, which is exactly the pattern that defeats LRU.

self_check.question: A stride-1 scan over an array of 8-byte doubles currently uses 64-byte blocks (compulsory miss rate $8/64$) with a 40-cycle miss penalty and a 4-cycle hit time. Doubling the block size to 128 bytes would halve the compulsory miss rate but raise the miss penalty to 70 cycles (wider transfer). Is the larger block an improvement for this workload, and would your answer change for a pointer-chasing traversal of a linked list?
self_check.answer:
For the stride-1 scan: $\text{AMAT}_{64} = 4 + (8/64)\times40 = 4+5 = 9$ cycles, versus $\text{AMAT}_{128} = 4 + (8/128)\times70 = 4+4.375 = 8.375$ cycles. The larger block wins here because the compulsory-rate benefit ($w/B$ halves) outweighs the extra transfer cost — exactly the spatial-locality case block size is meant to exploit.

For pointer chasing, the answer flips. Each node access has essentially no spatial locality with its neighbors in memory (the next node's address is unpredictable), so a fetched block is used for one access and then never revisited before eviction: the miss rate does not fall by $1/2$ the way it did for the array — it stays close to 1 regardless of block size, since almost every access is to a fresh block either way. The larger block then buys nothing but pays the full extra 30-cycle penalty on every miss, so $\text{AMAT}$ gets strictly worse. Block size only pays off when the access pattern actually has spatial locality to exploit.

key_points: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty; hit time is paid on every access, penalty only on misses.
Multi-level: the miss penalty of level k IS the AMAT of level k+1, so the model is a recursion.
Local miss rate divides by references reaching that level; global divides by all CPU references.
Core i7 (CENG331 slides): L1 32 KB 8-way 4 cyc, L2 256 KB 8-way 11 cyc, L3 8 MB 16-way 30–40 cyc, B = 64 B.
Cold misses answer to block size, capacity misses to cache size, conflict misses to associativity.
Row-major stride-1 access gives miss rate sizeof(elem)/B; walking a column gives miss rate 1.
tagline: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty, applied recursively L1→L2→L3→DRAM: a small top-level miss-rate cut beats a big DRAM latency cut.
tldr: Cache performance reduces to one equation, $\text{AMAT} = T_h + m\cdot T_p$, applied recursively so each level's miss penalty is the next level's AMAT. The leverage sits at the top of the hierarchy — the L1 miss rate multiplies everything beneath it — which is why restructuring code to cut a top-level miss rate typically beats buying faster DRAM. The three Cs (cold, capacity, conflict) identify which knob — block size, cache size, associativity — a given miss actually answers to, relative to an optimal-replacement baseline.

Patterson & Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design (RISC-V ed.), chapter “Large and Fast: Exploiting Memory Hierarchy”
